requirements.name: tools-sidebar explorer entry with focused overlay
key UX: The File Explorer still launches from the Tools sidebar and keeps the existing workspace gating logic.
Opening the explorer closes competing overlays and brings up a dedicated explorer surface instead of a cramped utility pane feel.
The new UI keeps the old open and close behavior, but visually frames the explorer as a primary workspace task.

requirements.name: mobile-first single-focus layout
key UX: The explorer now uses one single mobile-first flow across screen sizes instead of keeping a separate desktop split-pane logic.
Folder browsing, file preview, and file editing are distinct full-surface states so the user focuses on one task at a time.
The UI no longer expands into a desktop-specific dual-pane layout; the same single-column navigation model is reused everywhere.

requirements.name: header with breadcrumb path and clear session actions
key UX: The top area switches between a close action for the file list and a Back action for file detail states, with the current file context in the center.
Breadcrumb navigation remains available for folder browsing, while file edit actions are removed from the header so the top bar stays focused on navigation and context.
Primary file actions must live in the bottom action area instead of the header, keeping the mobile-first interaction model consistent.

requirements.name: icon-led directory and file list
key UX: Folder and file rows are now distinguished primarily through icons rather than literal `[dir]` or `[file]` labels.
Each row remains a full-width tap target and still maps to the same old behavior: folders navigate deeper and files attempt to open.

List rows stay on one line and show compact factual metadata such as size and file kind hints like text, image, or large-file state instead of policy-driven labels that only reflect old editability rules.

requirements.name: existing workspace-rooted navigation logic with cleaner hierarchy
key UX: The explorer still opens at workspace root and still supports entering folders and going upward through the current path hierarchy.
The Up behavior and workspace-relative path logic remain unchanged, but the UI presents parent navigation as part of the list and breadcrumb hierarchy.
Empty folders, loading states, and load failures are shown as deliberate explorer states instead of feeling like missing layout.

requirements.name: preview-first file detail flow for text files
key UX: When a workspace file is recognized as text, the UI moves from the file list into a dedicated preview screen before the user enters editing.
Source code, config files, docs, scripts, and other decodable text files all use the same focused reading and editing surface instead of being blocked by an extension allowlist.
The preview screen exposes Edit from the bottom action area, and the edit screen exposes Discard and Save from the same bottom action area.
requirements.design detail: Text-file support should be decided by real content and decoding success, not by a narrow extension allowlist. The explorer contract should represent whether a file is text, image, or another binary type so the UI can choose the correct detail screen.

requirements.name: text-file detection replaces editable allowlist gating
key UX: Any workspace file that can be decoded as text can be opened for preview and editing regardless of extension, including common source files such as `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.js`, `.jsx`, `.py`, `.go`, `.rs`, `.java`, shell scripts, and SVG source files.
Read-only or blocked states are no longer caused by a hand-maintained extension allowlist; if the explorer can open a file as text, the user can edit it inline.
The product stops treating code browsing as a special exception and instead makes remote code and document inspection a first-class explorer use case.
requirements.design detail: Replace allowlist-based `isTextEditable` decisions with content-based text detection and stable decoding rules so view and edit capability come from the same text classification path.

requirements.name: large text files use loading strategy instead of hard unsupported fallback
key UX: Large text files still open from the file list instead of dropping into an empty too-large dead end.
The explorer may load large text content progressively or partially, but the user stays in the same file context and can continue reading without being bounced back to the list.
Large-file handling is treated as a performance concern, not as a product rule that arbitrarily revokes file viewing or editing.
requirements.design detail: The old 256 KB cutoff should stop being the user-facing capability boundary. The backend and UI may use partial reads, progressive loading, or deferred full-content fetches for large text files, but those tactics should preserve the same file-open flow.

requirements.name: image files reuse the existing image preview pipeline
key UX: When the selected workspace file is an image, the explorer opens to an actual image preview instead of a generic unsupported or binary state.
Users can inspect the image at normal explorer size and tap through to the same larger preview interaction the app already uses for chat images.
The explorer does not invent a second image system; it reuses the product's existing image rendering and preview behavior so image files feel native across chat and workspace surfaces.
requirements.design detail: Explorer image detail should reuse the existing image display route and preview overlay patterns that already serve chat attachments, instead of introducing a separate bespoke viewer.

requirements.name: non-text non-image files use factual metadata-only detail states
key UX: When a workspace file is neither text nor image, the explorer shows a minimal detail state centered on useful facts such as file name, size, and type.
The UI avoids filler copy like explaining that a binary file cannot be edited inline; the screen should tell the user what the file is, not restate an obvious limitation.
Users can always back out to the file list from this detail state without losing explorer context.
requirements.design detail: Non-text non-image detail states should stay intentionally sparse and factual. They do not need a pseudo-read-only editor frame or generic explanatory prose.

requirements.name: sticky save flow and visible dirty state
key UX: Existing text files that are open in the explorer can be saved back to the workspace, and Save enables only when the draft is dirty and a save is not already running.
The redesigned UI gives unsaved changes a stronger visual presence through a persistent dirty indicator and a fixed bottom action area for Edit, Discard, and Save.
Successful saves update local state and file size, then return the user to preview mode for the same file instead of leaving them stranded in edit mode.
Failed saves keep the user in edit mode with their draft intact.
requirements.design detail: Save eligibility should follow the same text-file classification path as open and edit, instead of duplicating a separate extension-based policy gate.

requirements.name: unsaved-change protection across all edit exits
key UX: When a draft has unsaved changes, any attempt to leave edit mode must confirm before discarding work, including Back to preview, closing the explorer, opening another file, or navigating to another folder.
The dirty indicator remains visible before the confirm step so the warning does not feel abrupt.
If the user cancels the confirmation, they stay in the current edit state with the draft untouched.

requirements.name: chat-linked file opening with integrated explorer context
key UX: The existing `file://` handoff logic from chat remains unchanged and still rejects targets outside the active workspace.
The redesigned UI opens linked folders and files inside the same focused explorer flow, so chat-origin navigation feels native instead of bolted on.
Linked file opens should route into the same text, image, and large-file detail behaviors as direct explorer navigation instead of keeping a second-class fallback path.

requirements.name: tolerant AI-generated path recognition for file jumps
key UX: File jump parsing should become more tolerant of AI-generated path variants, including unstable `file://` prefixes, mixed slash styles, encoded separators such as `%5C`, and lightly wrapped path text.
The resolver should normalize noisy path strings into a stable workspace-relative target before deciding whether to open a folder or file.
Recognition should become smarter without weakening safety: ambiguous or outside-workspace targets must still be rejected instead of guessing aggressively.

requirements.name: workspace safety and race handling preserved behind the new UI
key UX: The redesign does not change the existing workspace-boundary protections, symlink filtering, or path validation rules.
The redesign also keeps the current race-safe async behavior where only the latest request is allowed to win.
Visually the explorer feels cleaner and more intentional, but its underlying safety model and state consistency rules remain the old ones.

requirements.name: preview and edit mode retain reading position
key UX: Switching between preview and edit for the same file should keep the user at the same approximate reading position instead of jumping back to the top.
The retained position should work in both directions: preview to edit and edit back to preview.
Position retention is scoped to the currently open file and should reset when the user opens a different file.
